title: Functions, statements and expressions
summary: Define functions with parameters and return values, learn the difference between statements and expressions that makes Rust's return values work, and write comments.

blocks.md: You have written one function many times: `main`. This lesson shows how to write your own, pass values in and get a value back. It also explains the single idea that makes Rust code look the way it does: almost everything is an **expression** that produces a value, and a semicolon turns an expression into a **statement** that does not.

blocks.title: Defining and calling a function
blocks.md: A function starts with `fn`, a name, parentheses and a body in braces. Rust uses **snake_case** for function and variable names: lowercase words joined by underscores. A function can be defined before or after the place that calls it; Rust does not care about the order.

blocks.output:
Hello from main
Hello from another function

blocks.title: Parameters
blocks.md: **Parameters** are the variables a function receives. Each one must have its type written out: Rust infers types inside a function body, but never in a function's signature. That is deliberate. The signature is a contract other code relies on, and spelling it out means the compiler rarely needs you to annotate anything else.

blocks.explain: The values you pass when calling, `5` and `'h'`, are the **arguments**. They must match the parameters' types exactly; passing `5.0` here is a compile error.

blocks.title: Statements and expressions
blocks.md:
This distinction matters more in Rust than in most languages:

- A **statement** performs an action and produces no value. `let y = 6;` is a statement, and so is a function definition.
- An **expression** evaluates to a value. `5 + 6` is an expression, and so is a function call, a macro call, and a **block** in braces.

Because `let` is a statement, you cannot write `let x = (let y = 6);` as you might in C (`x = y = 6`). But because a block is an expression, you can do this:

blocks.explain: The block's value is its last expression, `x + 1`. Note that `x + 1` has **no semicolon**. Adding one would make it a statement, the block would produce `()`, and `y` would be `()`.

blocks.title: The semicolon rule
blocks.md: A semicolon throws a value away. `x + 1` is the value 4; `x + 1;` is a statement whose value is `()`. Whenever a block or function should produce a value, its last line has no semicolon.

blocks.title: Return values
blocks.md: A function declares its return type after an arrow, `->`. The value returned is the **final expression** of the body. You can also leave early with `return value;`, which is the usual way to return from the middle of a function.
The most common beginner error with return values is a stray semicolon. Here is what the compiler says, and it even points at the fix:

blocks.output:
error[E0308]: mismatched types
 --> src/main.rs:1:24
  |
1 | fn plus_one(x: i32) -> i32 {
  |    --------            ^^^ expected `i32`, found `()`
  |    |
  |    implicitly returns `()` as its body has no tail or `return` expression
2 |     x + 1;
  |          - help: remove this semicolon to return this value

blocks.title: if is an expression too
blocks.md: Since `if` is an expression, it can choose a value. Both branches must produce the same type, because the variable that receives the value can only have one type. This replaces the `? :` operator of C and JavaScript.

blocks.explain: `&'static str` is the type of a string literal that lives for the whole program. You will meet the `'static` part properly in chapter 10; for now, read it as "a fixed piece of text".

blocks.title: Comments
blocks.md: `//` starts a comment that runs to the end of the line. Rust programmers write comments on their own line above the code they describe. A comment with three slashes, `///`, is a **documentation comment**: it describes the item below it, and `cargo doc` turns it into web pages. You saw these in the exercise starters.

blocks.title: Write a conversion function
blocks.md: Write `to_fahrenheit`, the opposite of `to_celsius` above: F = C × 9 / 5 + 32. Then the program should print `100°C is 212°F` and `-40°C is -40°F`.
hints: Float literals need a decimal point: `9.0`, not `9`.

blocks.title: A small toolbox of functions
blocks.goal: Write functions with parameters and return values, using expressions rather than temporary variables where you can.
blocks.behavior:
- `pub fn square(n: i64) -> i64`: n times n.
- `pub fn hypotenuse(a: f64, b: f64) -> f64`: the length of the longest side of a right triangle, √(a² + b²).
- `pub fn clamp_score(score: i32) -> i32`: the score limited to the range 0 to 100.
- `pub fn grade(score: i32) -> char`: `'A'` for 90 and above, `'B'` for 80 to 89, `'C'` for 70 to 79, `'F'` below 70. Clamp the score first.
hints: `f64` has a `.sqrt()` method: `(a * a + b * b).sqrt()`.
`clamp_score` can be an `if`/`else if`/`else` expression with no `return`.
In `grade`, start with `let s = clamp_score(score);`, then an `if` chain from the top grade down.
blocks.solution_explain: Every function body ends in an expression, so none needs `return`. `clamp_score` also exists in the standard library as `score.clamp(0, 100)`; writing it once yourself shows why an `if` expression works there.

questions.explanation: Every parameter needs a type, and the return type follows `->`.

hints: Look at the end of the last line inside the block.
questions.explanation: `x * 2;` ends with a semicolon, so it is a statement and the block's value is `()`. It does compile; `y` is simply `()`.
`let` is a statement. Arithmetic, calls, blocks and `if` all produce values.

questions.q: A function must be defined above the code that calls it.
questions.explanation: Rust does not care about order; a function can be defined anywhere in scope.

questions.q: Why does this not compile? `let n = if ok { 1 } else { "none" };`
questions.explanation: Both branches must have one type, because `n` can only have one type.

questions.q: A comment that documents the item below it starts with ___ (three characters).
questions.explanation: `///` doc comments become documentation with `cargo doc`.

points: `fn name(param: Type) -> Return { ... }`; parameter types are always written out.
Statements (like `let`) do something; expressions (arithmetic, calls, blocks, `if`) produce a value.
A block's value is its last expression; a trailing semicolon turns it into `()`.
A function returns its final expression; `return` leaves early.
`if` is an expression, so it can choose a value; both branches must have the same type.
`//` comments a line; `///` documents the next item.

terms.def: A variable in a function's signature that receives a value when the function is called.
The value passed for a parameter when calling a function.
An instruction that performs an action and produces no value, like let x = 5;
Code that evaluates to a value, like 5 + 6, a function call, a block or an if.
A comment starting with /// that documents the item below it and is turned into documentation by cargo doc.
